output.headline: Better blood pressure detection could help tens of thousands avoid heart attacks and strokes, says British Heart Foundation
output.standfirst: Largest study of its kind finds 59 per cent of cases in England undiagnosed and current approach ‘not fit for purpose’, with researchers calling for population-wide prevention
output.bodyHtml:
Better detection and treatment of high blood pressure could help tens of thousands of people avoid a preventable heart attack or stroke, the British Heart Foundation says, in response to research revealing that only half of people being treated by a GP for the condition in England have it under control, and that millions more are completely unaware they have the ‘silent killer’ condition.

The largest ever study of its kind has now established that most people with hypertension (59 per cent) are undiagnosed and in the dark, which raises their risk of stroke, heart attack and early death.

The Oxford University study of 1.4 million adults suggests that even among those who are diagnosed and receiving medication via their family doctor, blood pressure is out of control in 50 per cent of cases.

The researchers, whose findings are published in the journal BMJ Public Health, said they suggested the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure in England was ‘not fit for purpose’.

The study drew on data from the Our Future Health programme, examining people enrolled between 2022 and 2025 who had high blood pressure, defined as 140/90 mmHg or higher.

Related: ‘People should not feel guilty’: weekend lie-in may be good for you, experts say

The researchers were able to calculate that more than a third of adults (37 per cent) had high blood pressure, and that six in 10 of these were oblivious to their condition.

The research also pinpointed who is most affected: hypertension was almost 50 per cent more common in men than women (42 per cent compared with 29 per cent across all ages), and more common in older people.

Detection and control of high blood pressure improved substantially during the 2000s, the researchers said, though progress had plateaued since about 2011.

The researchers also identified ‘indications of worsening trends following the Covid-19 pandemic, possibly because disruptions to healthcare delivery may have had lasting effects’.

Wenyu Liu, a medical statistician at Oxford Population Health and lead author of the study, said: ‘While hypertension is largely a “silent killer”, the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure is not fit for purpose.

‘Our study highlights the prevalence of hypertension across demographics. This underscores the need for population-wide prevention strategies alongside targeted treatment for people at high cardiovascular risk.’

The researchers singled out ‘the most striking finding’ of the study as the high absolute number and the high proportion of people with undiagnosed hypertension. The study also found that only half of adults with high blood pressure treated by a GP were adequately controlled.

Dr Iain Turnbull, a GP, deputy chief medical officer at Our Future Health and a clinical research fellow at Oxford Population Health, set out the possible explanations for that figure, saying it was not clear why 50 per cent of patients who said they were taking blood pressure-lowering drugs had uncontrolled hypertension.

‘Blood pressure varies considerably between people, and some people need changes in dose or two or more different medicines before it is brought under control. Other health conditions and medications can affect blood pressure, too.

Related: AI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggests

‘There are also practical and social factors: side effects, complicated treatment regimens and competing health or life pressures can make medicines difficult to take consistently. Weight, diet, salt intake, alcohol and physical activity can also influence blood pressure.

‘So a high reading can have many explanations and shouldn’t be seen simply as a reflection of what an individual patient or healthcare professional has done.

‘There are also some important caveats … we did not have prescribing records available to independently confirm medication use, and a blood pressure measurement on one day does not necessarily represent someone’s usual blood pressure.

‘Even with those caveats, I wouldn’t regard 50 per cent as a satisfactory figure. Persistently high blood pressure increases the risk of stroke and heart disease, and bringing it under control reduces that risk.’

Prof Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, set out what he believes better detection could achieve, while saying the study ‘paints a concerning picture of the scale of undetected high blood pressure in the UK, and the challenges of keeping blood pressure under control in those already receiving treatment’.

He added: ‘Better detection and treatment could help tens of thousands of people to avoid a preventable heart attack and stroke. But to achieve this, we will need to rethink how we identify, treat and support those at risk so that blood pressure checks and effective treatment can benefit everyone.’
